title: Does chlorella (or spirulina) actually remove heavy metals?

grade.title: Small, uncontrolled, or single-source human evidence
grade.outcome: Chlorella and hair or blood mercury
grade.basis: One open-label study and one small before-after study. Hair is a limited outcome.

answerHtml: An open-label study reported lower hair mercury and a larger blood-mercury change than controls after 9 g/day of chlorella for 3 months. A second study, using a multi-ingredient product, reported lower hair metals at 90 days. No spirulina trial with a metal outcome was located, so spirulina is not graded. Neither chlorella study shows removal of a stored body burden with a clinical outcome.

sections.heading: Studies
sections.html:
• Maruyama 2018: open-label, 35 versus 23 healthy volunteers, 9 g/day for 3 months. Hair mercury fell (p=0.041). Blood change was greater than control (p=0.038). Hair n=33 and blood n=19 were analysed. Four of six authors were employed by a chlorella company. No PMID was found.
  • Merino 2019: 16 adults with titanium dental implants and/or amalgam, plus 21 controls. Hair mercury, silver, tin, and lead decreased versus baseline at 90 days. The product had more than one ingredient. PMID 31014007.

buyHtml:
The Heavy Metal Tested and Certified public register listed no licensees on 15 October 2026. That page reported 0 certified brands and 0 certified products, and it stated that no brand has completed the three-lot baseline. A specimen layout on the register is an illustration, not a licensee. This page does not name or rank any brand.

The program states that certification is a measurement of a product against a published limit, not a statement that the product is safe. If a licensee is later listed for this category, it will be on the register.
